newsitem.title: USA: SEC settles with First Montauk over Escambia Cty.
newsitem.headline: SEC settles with First Montauk over Escambia Cty.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission said Thursday it had reached a $227,092 settlement agreement with First Montauk Securities Corp to resolve allegations stemming from its sale of derivative investments to Escambia County, Fla.
The SEC said First Montauk agreed to give up $175,458 of commissions generated from the sales and to pay $51,584 in interest and a civil penalty of $50,000.
First Montauk did not admit to wrongdoing, its general counsel, Robert Rabinowitz said.

The broker-dealer, headquartered in Red Bank, N.J., consented to a cease-and-desist order, accepted censure and agreed to take corrective action including retaining an independent consultant to address problems related to its affiliate program, the SEC said.

The agreement settles SEC allegations that four former employees in First Montauk's now-defunct Houston office engaged in a scheme to park complex mortgage-backed derivatives with other dealers in order to move them off First Montauk's books.
The SEC said that allowed them to manipulate the price of the securities, charging excessive markups of over $1.85 million to First Montauk customers.

The commission also alleged that First Montauk failed to maintain acurrate books and records and incurred numerous net-capital deficiencies. It said that a registered representative in the Houston office made misrepresentations in connection with the sale of mortgage-backed derivatives to Escambia County.
The SEC also alleged that First Montauk's compliance procedures were inadequate to detect the scheme and that the company failed to reasonably supervise employees.
"We worked hard with our outside counsel with the commission to work through the problem. We came up with what we believe was a reasonable agreement for the firm," Rabinowitz said.
Rabinowitz said the four employees involved in the allegations acted without the knowledge of the firm or any of its principals.
The four also face criminal racketeering charges brought by the Escambia County prosecutor.
"We're cooperating with the prosecution," Rabinowitz said, adding that the four were long gone from the firm.

Separately, First Montauk agreed last October to pay $900,000 to Escambia County to settle a civil lawsuit that the county filed agaisnt First Montauk and other broker-dealers involved in the derivative sales.

The county invested $45 million of tax money in derivative securities between 1990 and 1994 and saw the value of its protfolio drop by half in late 1994, forcing it to delay public projects. The securities were finally sold at a $15 million loss.
The fiasco also resulted in the resignation of longtime Escambia County Comptroller Joe Flowers, who bought the securities. He pleaded no contest to malfeasance charges.
